analysis.one_liner: Has the U.S. Treasury buy one million bitcoins and hold them in a national reserve for 20 years.
analysis.headline: The bill to build a federal Strategic Bitcoin Reserve was introduced in March 2025 with 5 Republican cosponsors and has sat in the Senate Banking Committee with no hearing or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill directs the Treasury Department to buy 200,000 bitcoins a year for five years — 1,000,000 in all — and hold them in a new "Strategic Bitcoin Reserve," locked away for at least 20 years. After that, Treasury could recommend selling no more than 10% every two years, with proceeds going to pay down the national debt. It pays for the purchases by redirecting the first $6 billion a year of Federal Reserve earnings to Treasury, cutting the Fed banks' allowed surplus, and revaluing the Federal Reserve's gold certificates at today's gold price — a paper revaluation that would force the Fed banks to send Treasury a large one-time payment. The government's existing seized bitcoins would be moved into the reserve, states could store their own bitcoins there, and the bill affirms that no one's private bitcoin can be seized.
analysis.who_benefits: Existing bitcoin holders gain the most: a government buying roughly 5% of all bitcoins in existence — about 200,000 a year on a fixed schedule — would push the price sharply higher, and every coin already in private hands becomes more valuable. Crypto exchanges, custody firms, and miners also gain from the legitimization of a federal reserve built around their asset, and the bill guarantees a permanent government role for secure-storage and cryptographic-audit providers. If bitcoin's price rises over two decades, future taxpayers would also gain when the reserve is finally allowed to be sold to reduce the debt.

how_it_helps.text: Treasury must buy 200,000 bitcoins per year for five years, 1,000,000 total, and hold them in trust for the United States in a new Strategic Bitcoin Reserve.

All bitcoin in the reserve must be held at least 20 years, with no sales allowed in the meantime; after that, Treasury may recommend releasing no more than 10% of holdings per two-year period, with proceeds for reducing the national debt.
Bitcoin already held or seized by federal agencies must be transferred into the reserve rather than sold, and the government may acquire additional coins through forfeitures and gifts.

Purchases are funded by redirecting the first $6 billion of annual Federal Reserve net-earnings remittances for 2025–2029, cutting the Fed banks' allowed surplus from $6.825 billion to $2.4 billion, and reissuing the Fed's gold certificates at the current market price of gold, with the Fed banks remitting the difference to Treasury.

States may voluntarily store their bitcoin holdings in segregated accounts inside the federal reserve, and the bill affirms that the government cannot seize or restrict individuals' lawfully held bitcoin, including the right to self-custody.
The reserve must publish quarterly cryptographic proofs of its holdings, verified by an independent third-party auditor and overseen by the Comptroller General.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the downside risk. The money comes from Federal Reserve earnings that would otherwise flow to the Treasury's general fund, and from a one-time forced remittance triggered by revaluing the Fed's gold certificates — an accounting adjustment that creates a large paper payment but no new real wealth. Because the coins cannot be sold for 20 years no matter what, the public balance sheet would be locked into a famously volatile asset through any crash, with no ability to cut losses. If the price collapses, ordinary taxpayers absorb the loss; the buyers on the way up were the private holders who sold into the government's purchases.

drawbacks.text: The government would commit on the order of a hundred billion dollars or more to a single speculative asset on a fixed purchase schedule, and the 20-year no-sale rule means it cannot sell even during a severe crash, so taxpayers absorb the full downside while private sellers take the government's money on the way up.

The main funding mechanism — revaluing the Federal Reserve's gold certificates at market gold prices and forcing the Fed banks to remit the difference — is an accounting adjustment that manufactures a large payment on paper; the real cost shows up as reduced Federal Reserve earnings otherwise remitted to the Treasury.

Buying about 5% of all bitcoins in existence would transfer enormous wealth to the people who already hold the most bitcoin — large private funds, corporations, and early investors — and would leave the government dependent on the security and custody of an asset class it does not control.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest case for the bill: if bitcoin holds or grows its value over decades, the government ends up with an asset that can later be sold to reduce the national debt, at a bookkeeping cost that mostly shuffles Federal Reserve accounting. But that upside is entirely speculative, while the costs are concrete: a fixed, price-insensitive buying program worth on the order of a hundred billion dollars concentrated in one volatile asset, a 20-year lock that removes any ability to respond to a crash, and the largest windfalls going to existing large holders. A well-designed version would be smaller, phased by market conditions, and allow sales in a downturn; this one does none of those things.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Banking Committee in March 2025, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Cynthia Lummis introduced the BITCOIN Act of 2025 on March 11, 2025, joined by five Republican cosponsors: Senators Justice, Tuberville, Moreno, Marshall, and Blackburn.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on March 11, 2025, and the committee has taken no further action since.

The bill directs Treasury to buy one million bitcoins over five years, hold them for at least 20 years, and fund the purchases through Federal Reserve remittances and a revaluation of the Fed's gold certificates.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained anything concrete: the bill has not moved, though its introduction alone publicizes and legitimizes the asset its sponsors and the crypto industry hold.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; it sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans; no Senate Democrat has signed on, and the bill has not reached a vote where a partisan split could be measured.

industries.industry: Bitcoin holders (large funds, corporations, and early investors)
industries.note: A government buying roughly 5% of all bitcoins in existence on a fixed schedule would bid the price sharply higher, and existing private holders capture that gain without bearing the program's risk. The public would be buying at prices those holders' selling helps push up.

industries.industry: Crypto exchanges, custody, and digital-asset security firms
industries.note: The bill builds a permanent federal institution — secure cold-storage facilities, cryptographic audits, third-party verification, consultations with 'industry experts' — around their asset, guaranteeing government contracts and legitimacy. Section 10 also locks in the self-custody and non-seizure rules the industry has lobbied for.

The bill cuts the Fed banks' allowed surplus from $6.825 billion to $2.4 billion, redirects the first $6 billion of annual earnings remittances to bitcoin purchases, and forces a large one-time remittance from revalued gold certificates. The money comes out of earnings that would otherwise flow to the Treasury's general fund.

The bill revalues the government's gold certificates at the market price of gold, an implicit acknowledgment of gold's appreciation, but this is an accounting step with no direct effect on gold markets.

analysis.trajectory: With no hearing or markup more than mid-2025 after referral, the likeliest path is that the bill dies quietly in the Banking Committee. A federal bitcoin purchase program of this size would need support from the committee chair and leadership that does not exist in the record; even smaller digital-asset measures have moved separately. It could return in a future Congress in modified form, but as written it is very unlikely to reach the Senate floor this session.
